analysis.one_liner: Cuts steel imports to about one-fifth of the U.S. market and funds steelmaker modernization from auction proceeds.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it sat in two House subcommittees from mid-1989 until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped steel imports at 20.2% of the U.S. market for five years, with limits easing later and expiring in 1998, and would have capped each foreign country at 5% of the market [S2][S3]. Importers would have bought the right to bring in steel at government auctions, with the money going into a Steel Revitalization Fund [S2][S3]. The Fund would pay for loans, grants, and loan subsidies to steelmakers that submitted modernization plans requiring them to cut excess capacity and keep funding worker health care, retraining, and retiree pensions [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Banking committees, then to their trade and economic stabilization subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic steel producers and their roughly 125,000 remaining hourly workers, whose jobs and companies the bill's findings describe as threatened by imports and mounting debt [S3]. Steelmakers with approved restructuring plans would get direct loans, grants, or subsidized loans from the auction-funded Steel Revitalization Fund, on condition they cut excess capacity and continue funding worker health, retraining, and retiree benefit programs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps total steel imports at 20.2% of domestic consumption for quota years 1989-1993, rising to 25% in 1994, with per-country limits of 5%, aiming to restore the domestic market share the bill says imports eroded to the point that employment fell from 544,300 hourly workers in 1953 to 125,700 in 1988.

Uses auction proceeds, rather than general taxpayer money, to finance restructuring assistance to steelmakers, tied to plans requiring modernization, permanent capacity cuts, and continued funding of worker health care, disability, retraining, and retiree pension and health benefits.
Sets a firm end date: all quantitative restrictions terminate September 30, 1998, so the protection is explicitly temporary.

analysis.who_pays: Steel-consuming industries — automakers, appliance makers, construction, and machinery manufacturers — and ultimately their customers, who would pay higher prices as import quotas tightened supply. Importers would also bid for entry rights at auction, a cost that would be passed through in steel prices; foreign steel exporters would lose most of their U.S. market access.

drawbacks.text: Import quotas restrict supply and raise steel prices for every U.S. manufacturer that buys steel — autos, appliances, construction, machinery — and those costs reach consumers, a cost the bill does not address.
Auctioning scarce entry rights adds a further cost to imported steel on top of the quota, and those costs are passed on to steel buyers rather than absorbed by government.

Directing Commerce Department loans, grants, and loan subsidies to steelmakers is government support for one industry, and the bill allows grants for modernization (up to 10% of Fund money per year) that could prop up firms even if restructuring fails; economists generally find protection slows the adjustment it is meant to buy time for.
The restructuring assistance is discretionary with the Secretary of Commerce, raising the risk that aid flows to politically connected firms rather than the most viable ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a trade-off rather than a clear win. It offers genuine help to a shrinking workforce — steel employment had fallen by more than 400,000 jobs over three decades, and the bill requires companies receiving aid to keep funding retiree pensions and health care — but it buys that help by raising steel prices for the far larger population of steel-using manufacturers and their customers, and it does so through quotas, an auction tax on imports, and subsidies to a single distressed industry. The sunset in 1998 and the requirement that aided firms cut excess capacity temper the worst version of this trade-off, but the design still shifts costs from one concentrated industry to a broad, diffuse group of consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Banking committees on the day it was introduced, sent to their trade and economic stabilization subcommittees within a month, and then simply sat there until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 with no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Cardin introduced the bill on May 2, 1989, joined by 11 Democratic and 1 Republican original cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs committees.

On May 18, 1989 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Trade, and on June 1, 1989 to the Banking Subcommittee on Economic Stabilization; no markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed.
The bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, having never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Steel-using manufacturers and their customers, and foreign steel exporters, who kept the lower steel prices and fuller market access the quotas would have taken away. Domestic steelmakers got nothing from this bill, though the existing voluntary restraint agreement program continued limiting imports in the meantime.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 12 cosponsors split 11 Democrats and 1 Republican, so sponsorship was mostly but not entirely Democratic; however, no votes were ever taken, so the real partisan shape of support or opposition on the merits is unknown.

industries.note: Import quotas would guarantee these producers a locked-in share of the U.S. market for nine years, and auction-funded loans, grants, and loan subsidies would finance their modernization. Their gain comes directly from higher steel prices paid by the far larger population of steel-using firms and consumers, and the bill makes the quota-protected, federally assisted steelmaker the permanent channel for U.S. steel supply through 1998.

Quotas would protect remaining steel jobs, and restructuring aid is conditioned on companies continuing to fund worker health care, retraining, and retiree pensions — the bill's findings cite bankruptcies straining workers and federal pension guarantees. Steelworkers are the main ordinary people the bill was written for.

Import caps and auction-priced entry rights would raise the cost of their main input, and those costs flow to their customers. Their interest here runs alongside ordinary consumers', since both benefit from cheaper steel.

A 20.2% overall cap with a 5% per-country limit would shut most foreign producers out of the U.S. market, with the President directed to negotiate the wind-down of the existing voluntary restraint agreements into these harder quotas. Their loss is the domestic industry's gain.
